chapter.title: Face in, breath out

cards.body: The water is a bed, and right now you're lying on it with your face turned stiffly to the ceiling. This chapter is turning your face into the pillow. **The trick is to breathe out while you're in, not hold it**: a slow stream of bubbles from your nose and mouth, like sighing into the pillow, so the water becomes somewhere you exhale, not something you brace against.
cards.simpler: Think of the water as a bed. Right now you lie on it with your face turned stiffly up to the ceiling. This chapter is about turning your face into the pillow. **The trick is to breathe out while your face is in, not hold your breath.** Let a slow stream of bubbles out through your nose and mouth, like sighing into a pillow. Then the water becomes a place you breathe out, not something you brace against.

cards.prompt: Maya puts her face in the pool, holds her breath tight, and pops up after 2 seconds gasping. Her coach says one word. Which?

whyNot.a: That's a depth fix, not a breathing fix: her face was in fine. The gasp came from holding air, not from being too shallow.
whyNot.c: That's speed, not comfort: going quicker just means more panicked dunks. The gasp came from holding her breath, not from slowness.

cards.reteach: Holding your breath makes your chest tight and your brain shout to come up. Letting air out slowly through your nose and mouth does the opposite: it keeps water out and lets your body relax. Bubbles are the whole fix.

cards.title: Why bubbles, not breath-holding
cards.body:
When you hold your breath underwater, two things go wrong. Your chest tightens, and within seconds your brain sends a loud come-up-now signal. That signal is most of what feels like panic.

**Breathing out underwater switches that signal off.** A slow stream of air out of your nose and mouth keeps water from going up your nose, keeps your body loose, and uses up the air so you actually want the next breath in.

The rhythm is simple: in through your mouth above the water, out through nose and mouth below it. Eyes open the whole time. Goggles are allowed and welcome.
cards.simpler: Hold your breath under water and two things go wrong. Your chest tightens, and within seconds your brain shouts at you to come up. That shout is most of the panic. **Breathing out under water turns the shout off.** A slow stream of air from your nose and mouth keeps water out of your nose, keeps you loose, and uses up air so you want the next breath. Breathe in through your mouth above water, out below. Eyes open. Goggles welcome.

cards.title: The kitchen sink test
cards.body: Jonas, 34, could not put his face in a pool. So he filled the kitchen sink to the brim, took a normal breath, and put his face in while humming. The hum forced air out through his nose as a steady stream of bubbles. He lasted 8 seconds, lifted up, breathed in, and did it again 10 times. At the pool the next evening he did the same thing in chest-deep water, holding the wall, and was mildly annoyed it had taken him 34 years.
cards.simpler: Jonas, 34, could not put his face in a pool. He filled the kitchen sink to the brim, took a normal breath, and put his face in while humming. **The hum pushed air out through his nose as a steady stream of bubbles.** He lasted 8 seconds, lifted up, breathed in, and repeated 10 times. At the pool the next evening he did the same in chest-deep water, holding the wall. He was mildly annoyed it took 34 years.

cards.prompt: You're at the wall in chest-deep water, ready to put your face in. Which plan follows the chapter?

options.text: Big breath in, face in, hum steady bubbles out for 3 seconds, lift up, breathe in through your mouth.
Big breath in, face in, hold it as long as you can, lift up when it burns.
Face in, pinch your nose shut with one hand, count to 3, lift up.

whyNot.b: That's breath-holding, not breathing out: holding until it burns is exactly what makes the brain shout and the body stiffen.
whyNot.c: That's using your hand instead of your air: pinching keeps water out, but the stream of bubbles does that job for you, and your hands will be busy swimming later.

cards.reteach: The move is always the same: breathe in above, breathe out below. Humming makes the out-breath steady without thinking about it. Your nose stays unpinched because air flowing out of it means water can't flow in.

cards.title: The lift and the repeat
cards.body:
Lifting up to breathe is where most people rush. **Lift just enough to clear your mouth, breathe in through your mouth, and go straight back down.** No wiping your eyes, no shaking your head, no big gulp. If you wipe, you're telling your body the water is a problem.

Time it like this: about 3 seconds of bubbles, 1 second up to breathe in, back down. That rhythm is the same one you'll use when you swim a length later, so you're not learning a drill, you're learning the real thing.

If water goes up your nose, you stopped breathing out. Just start the hum sooner next time.
cards.simpler: Most people rush the lift. **Lift just enough to clear your mouth, breathe in through your mouth, and go straight back down.** No eye wiping, head shaking, or big gulp. Wiping tells your body the water is a problem. Aim for 3 seconds of bubbles, 1 second up, then down again. You will swim with that same rhythm later, so this is the real thing, not a drill. Water up your nose means you stopped breathing out, so hum sooner.

cards.body: Priya does 10 dunks and feels great, then realises she pinched her nose every single time without noticing. On dunk 11 with hands free, water shoots up her nose and she's back to square one. Spot it: if your hands are near your face at any point, your air isn't doing its job yet. Hands on the wall or on your thighs, and let the bubbles guard your nose.
cards.simpler: Priya does 10 dunks and feels great. Then she notices she pinched her nose shut every single time without meaning to. On dunk 11, hands free, water shoots up her nose and she is back where she started. **If your hands are near your face at any point, your air is not doing its job yet.** Keep your hands on the wall or on your thighs, and let the bubbles guard your nose.

cards.prompt: Your friend asks: "Why do swimmers blow bubbles underwater? Isn't that wasting air?" The chapter's answer is:

options.text: It's a signal to the lifeguard that you're fine.
Air going out of your nose and mouth keeps water out and keeps your body relaxed, so you want the next breath instead of panicking for it.
It makes you sink lower, which is faster for swimming.

whyNot.a: That's a nice idea for a lifeguard, not what the bubbles do for you: the point is your own nose, chest and calm.
whyNot.c: That's a floating question, not a breathing one: this chapter is about why letting air out keeps you comfortable with your face in, not about depth or speed.

cards.reteach: Holding your breath makes your chest tight and your brain panic. A slow stream of air out through nose and mouth stops water getting in, keeps you loose, and makes the next breath in feel natural. Bubbles out, breath in, repeat.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: **Breathe in above the water through your mouth, then put your face in and hum a slow stream of bubbles out through your nose and mouth for 3 seconds.** Lift just enough to breathe in again, hands off your face, and do it 10 times until the water stops being something you hold your breath against.
cards.simpler: **Breathe in above the water through your mouth, then put your face in and hum a slow stream of bubbles out through your nose and mouth for 3 seconds.** Lift just enough to breathe in again. Keep your hands off your face. Do it 10 times, until the water stops being something you hold your breath against and becomes somewhere you breathe out.

cards.body: Tonight, fill a sink or bowl to the brim. Face in, hum bubbles for 3 seconds, lift, breathe in through your mouth. 10 times, hands behind your back, eyes open.
cards.simpler: Tonight, fill a sink or bowl right to the brim. Put your face in and hum bubbles for 3 seconds. Lift, and breathe in through your mouth. **Do it 10 times with your hands behind your back and your eyes open.** Hands behind your back means your bubbles, not your fingers, are keeping water out of your nose.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now put your face in the water 10 times in a row, breathing out underwater each time and in above it, without wiping your eyes or holding your nose.
